transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE); Priya Sethi (Redwood SE); Marco Tan (Redwood CSM); Arielle Moreno (Mistral Head of Platform); Tomás Ruiz (SRE Lead); Nadia Chen (Security Architect); Elliot Park (Eng Manager)

Summary: (auto) Quick intake focused on failure modes and graceful degradation for Mistral's customer-facing payment assistant. Notetaker: Fireflies.ai (auto).

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey team, thanks for joining. I know Arielle set up this sync, appreciate you all making time. The goal today is to understand your tolerance for degradations, how you'd like traffic steered across regions, and whether Hosted or Dedicated/Private makes most sense for you.

[00:18] Arielle Moreno: Yeah thanks Jordan. High level -- Mistral runs a payments fraud-detect assistant, obviously low latency is critical - mostly us-east and eu-west traffic but we have spikes into APAC for merchants. We're worried about two things: what happens when a region degrades, and how the system behaves when we hit qps spikes or noisy tenants.

[00:34] Jordan Lee: Totally. Priya, want to take us through the typical options?

[00:38] Priya Sethi: Sure. Broad strokes: for region-level outages we offer routing policies that can fail over to a secondary region, or do partial degradation where we switch to a smaller model variant to keep latency within SLO. We also support circuit-breaker style backpressure: reject or queue, or return cached responses for repeated prompts. There are also Dedicated pools that give predictable throughput and private deployments for data residency.

[01:05] Tomás Ruiz: Quick q, Priya — when you say smaller model, is that automated? Like if we drop from a 70B to a 7B quantized model during failover, do you keep output quality thresholds?

[01:18] Priya Sethi: Good point. We do canary and quality gates — if you pin a degradation policy we will only shift to a degraded model variant if it passes your prompt-set evals or a baseline BLEU/ROUGE-like metric you define. It's configurable per route. There may be slight behavioral drift, we flag it in the console and emit traces to help you triage.

[01:45] Elliot Park: And how fast is the routing switch? We aim for under 500ms added latency on the request path during region steering — anything beyond that becomes user-visible.

[01:55] Priya Sethi: The switch is near-instant for control-plane decisions; data plane re-routing typically adds network RTT plus any KV cache warming. If you have prefix caching enabled, that helps — the runtime primes KV cache to reduce first-token latency. We also do adaptive batching to avoid long tail latency while maintaining throughput. So realistic hit depends on cache priming and replica warm state.

[02:25] Nadia Chen: A couple security questions: in Private deployments, do you manage KMS or can we bring our HSM? Also audit logs and SSO integration?

[02:33] Jordan Lee: For Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSMs; Redwood's control plane can be placed in your VPC or we can do air-gapped bundle installs. Audit logs, SAML SSO, RBAC are available across tiers. We'll share the SOC2 and ISO artifacts; note sometimes the auto-transcript spells KMS as K M S, but it's the same.

[02:56] Arielle Moreno: We definitely want to own keys if we go private for PCI-scope data. Hosted could still work if tokenization keeps sensitive payloads out, but we'd need clear guarantees on redaction and ephemeral storage.

[03:12] Marco Tan: (Redwood CSM) We usually recommend a hybrid pilot: run selected traffic on Hosted with enforced redaction plus a Dedicated pool for heavy tenants; if you need absolute control over keys, Private is the path.

[03:28] Tomás Ruiz: How do you handle backpressure during tenant spikes? We saw once a noisy tenant consume all qps and the rest of the app went into backlog.

[03:36] Priya Sethi: We have per-tenant quotas and token-level throttling. Also a multi-tier queueing system: if capacity is hit, requests can be shed, queued with a max wait, or degraded. The circuit-breaker can reject high-cost calls and route traffic to a fallback model or cached answer. You can set policies based on latency SLOs or cost budgets.

[03:58] Tomás Ruiz: If we reject, do you provide deterministic error codes so the app can trigger client-side fallback?

[04:04] Priya Sethi: Yes, we return structured error types and expose headers to indicate reason (backpressure|capacity|region-failover). We also surface approximate queue time.

[04:15] Arielle Moreno: For compliance we need evidence of request routing decisions for audits. Is that in the logs?

[04:21] Jordan Lee: All route decisions, model variant used, and any degradation steps are in the trace logs and the Console. For Private, logs can be forwarded to your SIEM; for Hosted we provide a log export and configurable retention. We'll include a sample audit extract.

[04:37] Elliot Park: Let's talk SLA. Our product SLAs promise 99.9% for peak regions. What do Redwood SLAs look like and is there credit for partial degradation?

[04:47] Priya Sethi: Our Hosted SLA varies by plan — typically 99.9% availability for API for standard plans; Dedicated SLAs are higher with reserved capacity commitments. For partial degradation events, we measure availability by successful response within your configured latency threshold; we can contract custom SLOs and runbooks for enterprise deals. Credits are proportional to downtime windows; we can map those to your contractual clauses.

[05:12] Tomás Ruiz: Are blackout windows for maintenance planned or can we request maintenance only during off-hours?

[05:18] Jordan Lee: For Dedicated and Private you control maintenance windows; Hosted has scheduled maintenance announced in advance with options for opt-out windows for enterprise.

[05:26] Arielle Moreno: Ok. A scenario: us-east has a partial outage — network flakiness causing 20% increased p99 latency. We want immediate failover for Charge API but keep low-latency reads served by a degraded model. Can you do per-route failover?

[05:39] Priya Sethi: Yes, per-route policies are the pattern. You can define route-level failover priorities. The console allows route definitions, and you can specify fallback sequences: e.g., primary -> secondary region (same model) -> secondary region (degraded model) -> cached response -> explicit error. That sequence is configurable with thresholds.

[05:59] Tomás Ruiz: How is data consistency handled if a request is served from a different region where a user session hasn't been replicated? We have session affinity concerns.

[06:08] Priya Sethi: We see two patterns: keep session affinity by routing sticky sessions via a session key, or accept eventual session consistency and surface warnings. We can integrate with your session store via direct VPC peering or private network routes so the runtime can consult a central store before choosing a region.

[06:28] Arielle Moreno: What's the story on KV cache warming? If we failover we'll suffer cold-start latency for large context windows, right?

[06:35] Priya Sethi: Correct — KV cache is per-replica; we have prefix caching and predictive pre-warm based on traffic patterns during failover. Our recommendation for strict SLOs is to warm a standby model in the secondary region; that's what Dedicated pools simplify because you can reserve capacity.

[06:54] Elliot Park: If we reserve capacity for peak we still want cost controls. Does Redwood support burstable reserved capacity?

[07:00] Jordan Lee: Yes, Dedicated has burst options. You can reserve baseline vGPU capacity and allow bursts to a shared pool with overage accounting. We also offer Optimize tooling to recommend quantization/profiles to cut 30-60% cost on non-critical routes.

[07:15] Tomás Ruiz: For our pilot, we want an experiment: route 5% of production writes to Redwood Hosted and the rest to Dedicated, and have automatic failover to Hosted if Dedicated goes down. Is that something achievable?

[07:26] Priya Sethi: That's exactly the kind of canary we support. Smart routing can route by weight and fallback to compatible model variants in hosted if dedicated is unavailable. One caveat: Hosted and Dedicated model variants must be pinned or compatible in the catalog; we'll help you pick the closest quantized variant.

[07:44] Arielle Moreno: Are you able to demonstrate a pilot that simulates region-level latency increase and show how the fallback chain behaves?

[07:51] Marco Tan: Absolutely. For pilots we run synthetic traffic with your top-100 prompts or example payloads; we can show failover events, traces, and delta in token costs and p95/p99 latency.

[08:05] Nadia Chen: Anything about encryption-in-flight and at rest that differs between Hosted and Private?

[08:11] Jordan Lee: Data in flight is TLS across all deployments. At rest, Hosted encrypts customer data with provider-managed keys by default but you can bring KMS keys for Hosted enterprise. Private gives you full control, obviously.

[08:22] Nadia Chen: For audit we need per-request ancestry: which model, kernel, quant profile, and which region. Do you log kernel-level details?

[08:31] Priya Sethi: Yes, we capture model version, quantization profile, kernel selection heuristic as part of the trace. Typically Kernel names might be encoded; we'll attach a mapping. Those traces can be forwarded to your SIEM or exported.

[08:46] Arielle Moreno: Quick question on developer ergonomics: if we do private deploy, how much operational overhead is expected?

[08:54] Priya Sethi: Private has an ops playbook, and we provide an installer and runbook. For air-gapped installs there's more work (images, network), but many customers treat it like any platform install — Redwood offers an ops-engagement to run the first deployment with you.

[09:10] Tomás Ruiz: Let's talk error modes. Can you walk through a concrete failure scenario and describe events and what we'd see in the console?

[09:18] Priya Sethi: Sure. Scenario: primary region goes into high latency due to network failure. The runtime detects p99 breach; automated policy triggers. First it increases batching for low-priority routes and applies circuit-breaker to heavy requests; second, it reroutes critical routes to secondary region; third, it switches non-critical routes to a degraded model variant. In the console you'll see an incident timeline, the affected routes, and the fallback path with times and error codes. You can also opt-in to runbooks that automatically create PagerDuty incidents.

[09:54] Elliot Park: What about fallthrough for streaming responses? If a stream starts in primary and then we switch mid-stream is that supported?

[10:03] Priya Sethi: Streaming is trickier mid-stream, since token-level state is in the KV cache. We recommend handling streaming connections per region; if a region degrades we emit an explicit stream error and client should re-open to the new endpoint. For some customers we provide a library to manage reconnection semantics and to stitch streamed partial responses, but that's custom.

[10:26] Arielle Moreno: Does Redwood have a way to simulate noisy tenants stealing capacity? We want to test tenant isolation policies.

[10:33] Priya Sethi: Yes, in staging we can inject synthetic tenants with high-cost patterns to validate quotas and circuit-breakers. We'll run a multi-tenant stress test as part of the pilot.

[10:45] Tomás Ruiz: When you route to fallback model is token accounting different? We can't have costs explode unexpectedly.

[10:52] Jordan Lee: Token accounting is explicit per-model. If a fallback uses a larger or smaller model cost will change; the Optimize tool provides cost impact estimates for different fallback chains. You can also set cost caps per-route to force an earlier cut to cached answers.

[11:10] Arielle Moreno: For immediate compliance needs, we need proof that Hosted deletes ephemeral logs after 30 days and that full request payloads aren't retained. Is that in your security docs?

[11:20] Jordan Lee: Yes, retention policies are configurable. Hosted defaults to a retention window we can shorten for enterprise; for Private you control retention. We'll attach the relevant sections in the security pack.

[11:31] Nadia Chen: Another one: if we have region steering and the secondary region is in a different legal jurisdiction, is there a way to block certain routes from leaving a region?

[11:41] Priya Sethi: Yes, you can tag routes as region-locked; the routing policy prevents egress for those. That's a common pattern for regulated workloads.

[11:50] Tomás Ruiz: Cool. Could you explain how the KV cache interacts with prefix caching and cold starts? If we have 8k contexts and long histories, does that change your failover profile?

[12:02] Priya Sethi: Longer contexts increase cold-start times because more of the KV needs to be primed. We recommend shorter prefix windows for latency-sensitive routes or keeping warm replicas in secondary regions for critical flows. Also fine-grained caching of repeated prompts helps a lot.

[12:22] Arielle Moreno: For the pilot scope we agreed to provide top-100 prompt set. What about telemetry? We need end-to-end traces correlated with internal request IDs.

[12:31] Marco Tan: We can ingest your request IDs via headers and surface them in traces in Console; recommended header is x-mistral-request-id. We'll also provide a tracing export to your APM.

[12:44] Elliot Park: Ok, nuts and bolts for pilot: can you quantify expected p95 add-on when failing over to eu-west from us-east? We need ballpark numbers for our SREs.

[12:55] Priya Sethi: If you route from us-east to eu-west, you're looking at network RTT: typically 60-120ms additional G depending on peering. Model inference time depends on model size and whether KV is warm; cold start could add 300-700ms for a large context. For a warmed standby model the delta is often <100-200ms. We'll run a bench with your payloads for precise numbers.

[13:20] Tomás Ruiz: Good. On the financial side, if we sign Dedicated with a 12-month commit and we never fully use the reserved headroom, is there a true-up or flexible reallocation?

[13:30] Jordan Lee: We have flexible committed usage tiers; we can reallocate within business units or offer credits for excess. There's also a conversion to on-demand for bursts. We can include a commercial clause for rebalancing after the first quarter if needed.

[13:47] Arielle Moreno: I want to flag the business constraint: our timeline is tight — pilot by September and production rollout before Black Friday. So we need clear runbook and a fast benchmark.

[13:58] Jordan Lee: Understood. We'll prioritize a rapid bench and a focused pilot.

[14:03] Nadia Chen: Last security item — does Redwood support customer-managed revocation or key rotation without downtime?

[14:11] Priya Sethi: We support key rotation with rolling re-encryption to avoid downtime; for HSMs we can do key swapping. There are patterns for zero-downtime rotations we can share.

[14:23] Arielle Moreno: Sounds good. Let's map next steps now.

[14:27] Jordan Lee: Action items recap — Priya will send region/capacity sheet; Jordan sends pilot terms & pricing; Mistral shares payloads and telemetry headers; we'll schedule bench and run the failover simulation. Anything to add?

[14:40] Tomás Ruiz: Add that we'd like a tenant-isolation stress test in staging.

[14:45] Marco Tan: Noted — we'll include noisy-tenant tests.

[14:49] Arielle Moreno: Also include an audit extract for retention and key ownership in the packet you send.

[14:55] Jordan Lee: We'll include that. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the runbook workshop.

[15:00] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hear of technical terms (e.g., 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cache'), some speaker attribution corrected post-hoc.
